title: Lesson 86: Capstone III: Evaluate, Harden, Deploy, Monitor
description: Growing the three-tier eval suite from production failures and gating releases on it, hardening against the excessive agency root causes of functionality, permissions and autonomy, staged canary rollout governed by an error budget, instrumenting agent traces and dashboards with named alerts, and the incident path with its postmortem ratio.

questions.question: Customer complaints and satisfaction are flat, but the rate at which humans edit the agent's drafts has doubled over three weeks. What does that signal?
options: Nothing actionable, because quality should be judged by customer satisfaction rather than edit metrics
A quality regression not yet visible to customers, since edit rate moves before complaints do
A threshold set too low, so the fix is to raise the edit-rate target to match the regional baseline
Retrieval drift that can only be fixed by rebuilding the search index from scratch
questions.explanation: Edit rate is the early-warning metric because it moves within days of a retrieval or prompt regression, well before complaint rates move. A rising edit rate with flat complaints is a system that got worse and nobody outside the team has noticed yet.

questions.question: A severity 3 quality incident is closed with several prompt edits and no new test coverage. What is wrong with that closure?
options: The incident should have been escalated a severity, since any post-launch quality drop is customer facing
Prompt edits kept in a console rather than version control make the closure unauditable
Nothing, because a prompt edit is faster to apply than a code change and the item has an owner
Every postmortem should add at least one eval case and at most one prompt change
questions.explanation: The ratio keeps incidents from becoming an unreadable pile of prompt edits with no test coverage. At least one eval case converts the incident into a regression test, and at most one prompt change keeps the instruction set comprehensible.

questions.question: The error budget burns most of its monthly allowance in two days after a bad change. What is the correct response?
options: Stop shipping changes until the budget recovers, rather than ship faster to fix things
Spend the remaining budget on the fix, since a budget exists to fund corrective changes
Roll the rollout back a stage and then resume shipping at the same rate
Raise the objective so the burn no longer breaches the documented threshold
questions.explanation: An objective is a budget to spend, and when it burns down the response is to stop shipping changes rather than to ship faster. Raising an objective to escape a burn defeats the purpose of having one.
